title: Wings are enough
hookLine: the renunciant is content like a bird that takes only its wings

cards: Moving day. Boxes everywhere. Things forgotten under the bed, in the back of a closet, each one asking: keep me?
And each one, kept, gets carried to the next place. Outside the window, a small bird sits on a branch. It takes off, carrying nothing but the wings it flies with.
In the second long discourse, after the first fruits, the Buddha describes the monk's daily life, and lands on that bird.

teach.b: He walks the king through the training step by step. First, the moral conduct, all those small things. Then guarding the senses: seeing a form, not grabbing at its features.

Then mindfulness and clear knowing in everything: walking forward and back, looking ahead and to the side, bending and stretching, eating and drinking, even in the toilet, falling asleep and waking. And then this.
How, great king, is a monk content?

teach.h: A ROBE FOR THE BODY, FOOD FOR THE STOMACH
teach.b: He's content with a robe to protect his body and almsfood to keep his stomach going, and wherever he goes, he takes only these.

teach.h: A BIRD WITH ONLY ITS WINGS
teach.b: Just as a bird, wherever it flies, flies with its wings as its only burden. The Pali word is santutthi: contentment, being satisfied with what's enough. It's not total poverty.
He has a robe and a bowl; the bird has wings. It isn't a contest to own nothing. It's carrying only what the flight needs.

teach.h: CONTENT, THEN THE FOOT OF A TREE
teach.b: Then someone with this virtue, restraint, mindfulness and contentment goes to a quiet place, a forest, the foot of a tree, a mountain cave, sits cross-legged, and sets mindfulness in front.
That's where the next fruits begin.
The order matters. Contentment comes before the deep meditation, not after. A mind still packing and unpacking boxes can't sit still under a tree.
And the Buddha offers this lightness to a king who owns elephants, palaces and an army, as a fruit visible here and now.

how: Buddhist monastics traditionally keep only a few requisites (robes, bowl, and a small set of necessities), and contentment is taught to lay people too as a quality to cultivate alongside generosity.

o: a calm that comes after meditation
owning nothing at all, by vow

games.q: wings are enough: tap the pairs.
p: flies with its wings as its only burden

s: the monk in DN 2 owns nothing at all
he has a robe and a bowl: what the flight needs, like the bird's wings.
contentment comes before the deep meditation in the discourse's order
with contentment in place, he goes to the foot of a tree and sits.
the bird simile is offered to a king who owns palaces and an army
as a fruit of practice visible here and now.

games.q: you've just gone forth with a robe and a bowl. a supporter offers you a second robe, a trunk and a spare bowl for your travels. what does the bird simile suggest?
o: take only what the journey needs.
refuse even the robe you have.
games.why: the monk is content with a robe for the body and food for the stomach, and takes only these wherever he goes, like a bird with its wings.

practice: Notice what you're carrying right now, tension in the shoulders, a plan for later, a worry from this morning, and name each one gently.
Ask whether this flight needs it, and if not, set it down for the length of the sit: a body, a breath, wings.

wordCard.voice: Santutthi. Contentment, being satisfied with what's enough, like a bird with its wings as its only burden.

orig.note: Pali santutthi: contentment, being satisfied with what's enough.

carryVoice: Your line: only what the flight needs. A robe, a bowl, a pair of wings. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Digha Nikaya 2, Samaññaphala Sutta, the passage on contentment
